decisions.reason: SOL keeps the attendants’ actions and the palace’s maze-like corridors while breaking up a cumbersome sentence.
SOL drops the narrator’s inward muttering, which the Korean explicitly includes.
SOL preserves the confirmation and the Emperor’s characterization.
“Youngest brother” conveys the Korean without BASE’s redundant “youngest younger brother.”
The Korean states a general principle in the present; SOL shifts it to past tense.
SOL changes the unseen dangers into dangers the Emperor personally cannot see and weakens the source’s bloody-storm image.
“Common people” naturally conveys 백성 here.
SOL keeps the unnatural death as a pretext for another rebellion without BASE’s added “perfect.”
“Would look the most natural” keeps the point about poisoning while sounding idiomatic.
The source says poison of that caliber would be difficult to obtain; SOL changes this to finding poison potent enough to overcome the ring.
SOL omits the Myriad-Poison Ring, an explicitly named item in the Korean and binding glossary.
SOL keeps the thought that the action has bought them time.
SOL recasts the rhetorical question naturally and sets up the answer that follows.
The concise “No” answers SOL’s preceding question without changing the meaning.
The Korean says the connection was certainly deep; SOL drops the certainty.
SOL preserves the need to protect the prince despite the risk to the ring.
“The one person who could hold it together” naturally conveys his role as the faction’s rallying center.
The Korean says Prince Shangshan and his party disappeared; SOL narrows the group to his attendants.
SOL keeps her quiet gaze and the impression her face would leave after one meeting.
The name So Gyo appears in the following dialogue; removing this separate introduction avoids repetition.
SOL preserves So Gyo’s calm response and her formal statement about carrying out the Emperor’s orders.
“Can’t fault her loyalty” keeps the narrator’s dry inward reaction.
SOL retains the awkward nod and the dialogue, placing the action naturally before he speaks.
“Guide me out” is a natural rendering of the order to lead him out.
SOL keeps the sarcastic distinction between being guided and being watched and expelled.
The pronoun clearly refers to So Gyo in context.
The added reference to the way they came is clear from the exchange and preserves her point that he remembers.
“Checking my escape route” naturally conveys that he had looked ahead in case of the worst.
Removing the separate dialogue setup avoids repetition; the incredulous reply remains in the next hunk.
The Korean explicitly describes him asking with an incredulous expression; SOL’s “stared at her” loses that reaction.
SOL states naturally that the route into the palace differs from the route out.
SOL omits that Young Master Jin is a martial artist, an explicit part of So Gyo’s address.
The Korean says a word flashed through his mind; SOL changes it to a possibility.
SOL keeps her nod, her resuming the lead, and his hurried, still-shocked response.
The shock is already conveyed in the preceding sentence, so the separate repetition is unnecessary.
The sentence break preserves the same image and exasperated voice.
“No fewer than three” preserves the Korean emphasis that there were as many as three, rather than asserting exactly three.
“At close range” and “even by a conservative estimate” preserve the guarding distance and low estimate.
SOL keeps the incredulous reaction to the palace’s mechanisms and formations.
SOL keeps the point that an Emperor needs security but that it has limits.
The abnormal defenses are stated in the next hunk, so this separate repeated sentence is unnecessary.
SOL combines the abnormal defenses with the comparison to the Emperor without changing the sense.
“Maybe he was afraid, too” preserves the narrator’s speculation.
“Dismembered or beheaded” naturally renders the two described forms of killing without asserting that each victim suffered both.
“His own blood relatives” conveys the blood-related members of the imperial family.
“All of them had died” preserves the fact without changing its scope.
SOL keeps the coup’s violation of the natural order and the single man’s command.
The added emphasis on “didn’t” suits the rhetorical point and does not alter the meaning.
SOL preserves the contrast between the Emperor’s status and his identity as a Supreme Peak master.
“Considering his age” naturally conveys that he looked much older than his young age warranted.
The Korean specifies innate talent; SOL broadens this to talent in general.
SOL’s “master” intensifies the Korean’s “learn” martial arts.
SOL drops the martial world, explicitly named in the Korean and required by the glossary for 강호.
SOL preserves both his fear of assassination and his nightmares in natural phrasing.
“Certainly possible” better preserves the Korean’s claim that the guess is quite plausible; SOL weakens it.
“Understand a little” naturally conveys his vague understanding of the Emperor’s feelings.
SOL changes the narrator’s claim that he had to defeat them into a claim that they had to be stopped.
SOL drops the source’s explicit “countless” dead.
SOL keeps the narrator’s rhetorical question about the Emperor’s state of mind.
SOL preserves the silent, deepening walk into places he could not make sense of.
“Starting to get a bad feeling” naturally conveys his growing unease.
The Korean says she spoke as she turned; SOL adds that she spoke before he could say more.
Her “괜찮습니다” permits him to ask; SOL replaces that response with reassurance that belongs to the following exchange.
SOL keeps her reassurance that no misfortune will happen and her request that he follow.
“Was quiet” preserves the pause before he clicks his tongue.
SOL keeps the mind-reading joke in natural dialogue.
SOL preserves her observation that his breathing had become slightly uneven.
SOL conveys the importance of breath control for a martial artist without changing the claim.
“Less than a breath” naturally conveys that fights can be decided in an instant.
The provocative tone and So Gyo turning away are incorporated in the next hunk.
SOL preserves the narrator’s sense that her manner was challenging and his thought that she was picking a fight.
“First Rate at best” and “lecture me” naturally preserve his dismissive reaction.
The referent is clear, and SOL preserves that she serves the Emperor and he is in enemy territory.
“Isn’t” preserves the thought without changing its meaning.
“No point arguing” naturally conveys that talking further would be pointless in this exchange.
SOL keeps the faint sound coming from a dark corridor among branching paths.
“An irritated voice” preserves the speaker’s irritation.
The reordered exclamation preserves the woman’s insult and indignation.
SOL keeps So Gyo blocking him and his response of sharpening his senses.
“Every clue I could get” naturally conveys the need to find as many clues as possible.
SOL preserves the warning shout and her cold, warning glare; the name is clear from context.
So Gyo’s glare is already included in the preceding hunk, so the repeated description can be removed.
SOL preserves his increased certainty that she is hiding something outsiders must not see.
Pretending not to understand naturally conveys his feigned ignorance.
SOL keeps his complaint and question in spontaneous dialogue.
“Might not sleep tonight” preserves the simple exaggeration without changing its sense.
SOL keeps her stern expression and integrates the shouted command into the sentence.
The command “Out!” is included in the preceding hunk, so this separate line is redundant.
The next sentence already conveys that the attack happened in an instant.
The added “In an instant” carries the timing into the description of the blades.
SOL drops the source’s image of masks as black as the darkness.
SOL loses the narrator’s heavy, lowered voice and the immediacy of being surrounded in a flash.
So Gyo says he must turn around and leave quietly; SOL changes that to coming with her.
“Wanted to look” preserves his explanation that he heard a strange noise and went to investigate.
SOL preserves her question about whether he is defying the Emperor’s will.
SOL preserves both possible reasons for their icy expressions and his quiet surrender gesture.
“Dismissed the assassins” naturally conveys her ordering them to withdraw.
“Invite any more danger” preserves his decision not to provoke further trouble.
The source says he had already achieved his limited objective; SOL narrows that to learning what he needed to know.
SOL combines the clearly heard sound with the woman’s sharp cry, whose identity is specified immediately afterward.
The sharp cry is already included in the preceding hunk, so repeating it separately is unnecessary.
“Had reminded me” shifts the source’s simple recollection into a past-perfect sequence.
“Practiced” adds an implication absent from the source’s description of her sweet, seductive voice.
“What was her name?” naturally conveys the narrator searching his memory.
“The Emperor had taken from” directly preserves that the Emperor took the concubine from the City Lord.
